name: Adam Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This time of year it's pruning, so I'm out in the rows by half seven with loppers and a saw, and Stefan, the head grower, walks behind me and fixes my cuts. In spring it's frost nights, sitting up with an app that pings when the temperature drops near the blossom, and spraying against scab, which is a fungus that marks the apples. Harvest is September and October, and that's sixty pickers, bins everywhere and the cold store humming. I love harvest, everyone's tired and happy. What wears me out is pruning, because I'm still not good at it and every tree is a little test I keep failing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the orchard and how you got there.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's Fairbank Orchards, about seventy hectares of apples and pears, owned by Margaret Lindell, who's fifty-eight and grew up there. We sell to wholesalers and a juice company, and the bruised ones go for juice. I've been there two years, after a few years in a warehouse. Stefan says I'll be a decent pruner in about five more winters, which is his idea of a compliment.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI tools, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use them all day. A scab forecast app that tells me when to spray, a frost alarm, and an app that counts the little fruitlets from photos so we can guess the crop. I ask a chatbot about spray labels and rules, then double-check with Stefan. At home it's me and Mia, she's a vet at a small animal practice. My gran left me some money and I bought a small flat with it that I rent out, so we're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a little disappointing, honestly. But fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, it just isn't a miracle. The scab app alone saved us two sprays last spring, which is real money. I'd post about that, actually, because farmers like hearing what saves money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd keep pushing the tools, because I'm the one here who uses them. That's my little edge while I'm still bad at pruning. If AI's a flop, I've got to find a different edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the apps and build a small juice brand from our seconds, the apples that aren't pretty enough for the shops. I'd ask Margaret if I can rent the press two weekends a month and put in about five thousand of my own money for bottles and labels. Farm markets and a few cafés to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why juice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we throw away money every October. There's a pile of apples by the cold store every autumn that would make better juice than anything in the shops. We just tip it on the compost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Stefan say about the juice idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say concentrate on the pruning first. Then he'd taste it and tell me it needs more Bramley in it, which is his way of saying yes.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still a good tool, just not a miracle, since the scab forecast saved two sprays last spring. I'd post about it, because farmers like hearing what saves money.
S0.think: I think I'd keep pushing the tools, because using them is my small edge while I'm still bad at pruning. If AI is a flop, I'd need a different edge.
S0.do: Keeps learning the farm apps and starts a small juice brand from the orchard's seconds. Rents the press two weekends a month and puts in about five thousand of his own money for bottles and labels.
S0.quote: There's a pile of apples by the cold store every autumn that would make better juice than anything in the shops. We just tip it on the compost.
S0.fieldNote: He sees tools as his advantage while his hands-on skills catch up, which is why the quiet picture disappoints him slightly. He found a business idea in waste within seconds. His head grower appears in every story as the person whose approval he wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my favourite one, I'll be honest. Change, but with time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for orchards if we're smart about it. Picking is the hardest job to fill, and if robots take some of it, fine, but we have to help the pickers find something else. I'd say it at the growers' group and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in the right place. Picking robots work best in orchards where the trees are trained flat, like a wall of fruit, and nobody here knows much about that yet. If I learn it, I'm useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Margaret to let me replant two blocks as fruit walls next winter, ready for robot picking in four or five years. I'd go and see a robot picker working at one of the big orchards in the spring. And I'd keep the juice going and put another five thousand into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the night before harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Margaret say about replanting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say trees are a twenty-five-year decision, and she's right. Planting an orchard for a robot that doesn't exist yet is a bit like buying shoes for a baby that isn't born. But someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pickers, especially the ones who come every year. Some of them earn their whole year's savings with us in eight weeks. Margaret would want to look after them, but she's got to make the numbers work.

S1.say: I'd say this is good for orchards if we're smart, since picking is the hardest job to fill. If robots take some of it, we must help the pickers find something else, and I'd say so at the growers' group and online.
S1.think: I think I'm in the right place, because picking robots work best with trees trained flat like a wall of fruit. Nobody here knows much about that yet, so learning it would make me useful.
S1.do: Asks his boss to replant two blocks as robot-ready fruit walls next winter and visits a large orchard using a robot picker in spring. Puts another five thousand into his juice business.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, like the night before harvest.
S1.quote: Planting an orchard for a robot that doesn't exist yet is a bit like buying shoes for a baby that isn't born. But someone has to.
S1.fieldNote: He sees this picture as his opportunity and has clearly already read about fruit-wall orchards. His concern for the seasonal pickers is genuine but practical, framed around his boss's numbers. The baby shoes line captured both the risk and his appetite for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a sprint, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we need to be practical. Help people move, keep the food coming, don't panic. I'd say it at work and probably post a lot about what I was seeing on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being early only buys me about a year. Orchard owners would just rent fleets of robots from big companies, and the companies would send their own people. I'd be the clever junior who knew a lot about apps, and that would be worth nothing very quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away to the companies that rent out farm robots, as a local field person, and try to get in before everyone else does. I'd put some savings into a fund that holds shares in robot and AI companies. And I'd keep a big chunk in cash, because in a change that fast you want to be able to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd be moving fast, which I like better than sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years you can't build anything, you can only jump on something moving. In two years I'm not planting fruit walls. I'm running for the last bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Mia's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up, actually. Everyone thinks vets are safe because it's hands-on. In this picture nothing is, and she's spent seven years training.

S2.say: I'd say it's a big change and we need to be practical: help people move, keep the food coming, and don't panic. I'd say it at work and post about what I saw on the ground.
S2.think: I think being early only buys me about a year, because orchard owners would rent robot fleets and the rental companies would send their own staff. Being the junior who knew the apps would soon be worth nothing.
S2.do: Applies straight away to farm robot rental companies as a local field worker. Puts some savings into a fund holding robot and AI company shares and keeps a large amount in cash.
S2.feel: Anxious, but steadier for moving fast.
S2.quote: In two years I'm not planting fruit walls. I'm running for the last bus.
S2.fieldNote: Even this adaptive, comfortable young man saw his advantage shrink to about a year in the fast picture. His instinct is to jump on the moving thing and keep cash ready. His deepest worry was his partner, whose long vet training he had assumed was safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so let's plan. Small growers should be able to get cheap loans or share robots, not just the big estates. I'd say that at the growers' group, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd start my own business doing robot picking for small orchards that can't buy their own. Buy two machines, run them up and down the valley at harvest, charge per bin. It might only work for three or four years, but those would be good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the flat in the first year and use that money, plus a loan, to buy two picking robots once they're proven, maybe year two. I'd spend the first year learning everything about them, going to the trials, getting to know the growers. I'd keep the juice as a little sideline, and keep my job at Fairbank part time while it got going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be putting a lot of money into machines that might be out of date fast. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. So is every tractor anyone ever bought. You don't buy a machine because it'll last forever, you buy it because it pays for itself first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mia say about selling the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask me to show her the numbers twice. And then she'd say yes, because she's braver than me, she just hides it better.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so plan. Small growers should get cheap loans or share robots rather than leaving them to big estates, and I'd say so at the growers' group.
S3.think: I think I'd start my own business doing robot picking for small orchards that can't buy their own machines. It might only work for three or four years, but they'd be good years.
S3.do: Sells his rental flat in the first year and, with a loan, buys two proven picking robots in year two. Spends the first year learning the machines and meeting growers, keeping the juice sideline and a part-time job at the orchard.
S3.quote: So is every tractor anyone ever bought. You don't buy a machine because it'll last forever, you buy it because it pays for itself first.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is long enough for him to turn the change into a business, and he was ready to sell an asset to do it. He knows the machines may age fast and treats that as normal farm thinking: a machine just needs to pay for itself. His partner is his check on risk, and he credits her courage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Margaret would be sixty-eight. That changes things at Fairbank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this well, so no excuses. Train people, help small farms buy in, and keep the country looking like countryside. I'd say it everywhere I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd want to own some of the orchard by then. Margaret's son doesn't want it. If robots are going to pick the apples anyway, I'd rather be the one who owns the trees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the robot picking business around year three, when the machines are proper. Then I'd save hard and talk to Margaret about buying one block of the orchard, maybe ten hectares, over five or six years. I'd keep the juice brand growing, because people will still pay for an apple with a story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the one where I can see the whole path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change, compared with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between being a worker and being an owner. With two years I'm running for a bus. With ten I can buy the bus. Sorry, I keep doing transport jokes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Mia, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably get married and start a family in the steady years, before the big change. She'd keep vetting while she can. We'd have the orchard block as something that's ours, whatever happens.

S4.say: I'd say there's time to do this well, so no excuses: train people, help small farms buy in, and keep the countryside looking like countryside. I'd say it everywhere I could.
S4.think: I think I'd want to own part of the orchard by then, since the owner's son doesn't want it. If robots will pick the apples anyway, I'd rather be the one who owns the trees.
S4.do: Starts the robot picking business around year three, when the machines are proven. Saves to buy a ten-hectare block of the orchard over five or six years and keeps growing the juice brand.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, able to see the whole path ahead.
S4.quote: With two years I'm running for a bus. With ten I can buy the bus.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years moves him from riding the change to owning land, which is a bigger ambition than anything he described in the faster pictures. He timed each step carefully, waiting until year three for proven machines. Marriage and children came up here, placed deliberately in the steady years before the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd be ruined, I'd probably land on my feet. Because there's no time to build anything, everyone just scrambles, and the pickers and the older workers get trampled. What would help is cheap loans so small growers can share robots, and clear safety rules so insurers will actually cover them in orchards.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the trees. An orchard is a twenty-five-year decision. If nobody knows what the next ten years look like, nobody plants, and in a few years there's no fruit to argue about.

headlineQuote: If robots are going to pick the apples anyway, I'd rather be the one who owns the trees.
portrait: Adam Costa is a 27-year-old junior on a seventy-hectare apple and pear orchard, still struggling with pruning but quick with every app on the farm. He owns a rented-out flat left by his grandmother, lives with his partner Mia, a vet, and has a juice side business in mind for the orchard's waste apples. He is pragmatic in his politics and comfortable with risk, seeing Steady Disruption as his best chance to learn robot-ready orchards. AGI by 2028 shrinks his advantage to about a year and makes him anxious, mostly for his partner and the pickers. With five years he would sell the flat to start a robot picking service, and with ten he would aim to own part of the orchard.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because nobody would have time to build anything and the pickers and older workers would be trampled in the scramble.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans so small growers can share robots, and clear safety rules so insurers will cover robots in orchards.
